You use indefinite pronouns and adjectives correctly (chaque, chacun, certains, aucun, n’importe qui, quiconque, tel) to talk about unspecified people and things, especially in cultural contexts.
No antique dealer would give ten euros for them.
Some visitors were crying, others were taking photos.
Distinguish the adjective “chaque” from the pronoun “chacun / chacune”.
Use certains, plusieurs, quelques / quelques-uns, d’autres.
Use aucun / aucune and nul / nulle with “ne”.
Use the series “n’importe qui / quoi / où / quand / quel” and “quiconque”.
Tuesday, 9 January 2035. Claudine Lacroix, chief curator of the Lyon Museum of Fine Arts, comes to Odile’s flat to choose objects for the exhibition about the waltz. Julien and Isabelle welcome her.
Thank you for having me. I’d like to see every object, even the smallest. Each one has its place in the story.
I’m warning you: none of these objects is worth anything. A harmonica, a cassette, some notebooks…
Museums are full of ordinary objects. What matters isn’t the object, it’s what was done with it.
Here are my father’s logbooks. There are twenty-three of them. Some are damaged, others almost new.
Wonderful. Could I borrow several? Not all of them, just a few.
Take whichever you like. But I care about one thing: don’t let just anyone touch them.
I promise you. Whoever handles them will wear gloves. And the harmonica?
That comes with a condition. My daughter wants to be able to take it back whenever she likes, to play three notes.
(she laughs) No museum in the world has ever accepted such a clause. But all right. It will be our secret.
And my mother’s armchair? I don’t know if anyone will want to see it.
Everyone will want to see it. I’ll put it in the middle of the room, with the blue shawl. Some will look at the display cases; others will stop in front of it.
Mr Moreau, a waltz that thousands of people have whistled without knowing each other… Believe me, people will come from anywhere.
“Chaque” is an ADJECTIVE: it comes before a noun. “Chacun / chacune” is a PRONOUN: it replaces the noun:
Chaque visiteuse a reçu un cartel.
Chacun de vous a rempli le silence.
“Chaque” cannot stand alone: “Ils ont reçu un cadeau chaque” ✗ → “chacun un cadeau” or “un cadeau chacun” ✓.
Certains carnets sont abîmés. Certains pleuraient.
Plusieurs visiteurs sont revenus. J’en ai lu plusieurs.
With pronouns of quantity, don’t forget “en”: “J’en emprunte plusieurs.” “J’en prends quelques-uns.” (= of them).
“Aucun / aucune” (no, none) and “nul / nulle” (formal) are used with “ne”, without “pas”:
None of these objects is worth anything. (pronoun)
No antique dealer would give ten euros for them. (adjective)
Nobody knows what she did on the quay. (formal = personne)
She has no desire to leave.
Don’t put “pas” next to aucun: “Il n’a pas aucun ami” ✗ → “Il n’a aucun ami” ✓. “Aucun” is almost always singular.
The “n’importe” series expresses total indifference (“any, it doesn’t matter which”):
Ne les laissez pas toucher par n’importe qui.
Il viendra du monde de n’importe où.
Elle veut le reprendre n’importe quand.
“Quiconque” (whoever, formal) can introduce a clause: “Quiconque les manipulera portera des gants.” = Whoever handles them will wear gloves.
Such a clause is rare. (tel = such, agrees)
Ordinary objects. (quelconque = nothing special, after the noun)
One must respect others. (autrui = one’s fellow humans, formal)
Some were watching, others were whistling.
You have learnt almost all the B2-level indefinites. In the exam, use them to avoid repeating “les gens” and “tout le monde”.
“None of these objects is worth anything.”
Aucun de ces objets n’a de valeur.
Aucun de ces objets n’a pas de valeur.
Pas aucun de ces objets a de valeur.
Some were crying, others were taking photos.
Whoever handles them will wear gloves.
Combien de carnets de bord Henri a-t-il laissés ?
Selon Madame Lacroix, qu’est-ce qui compte ?
Ce qu’on a fait de l’objet
Quelle condition pose la fille de Julien ?
Avoir une entrée gratuite pour sa classe

The flight to Dakar left Lyon on Saturday 16 December 2034, at seven in the morning. On board were three passengers any observer would have found strange: a woman checking a spreadsheet headed “Honeymoon” on her phone, a man in a grey suit holding a violin case on his knees like a child, and a sixty-six-year-old primary teacher looking out of the window without a word, her hands clasped around an old photo.

Mariama hadn’t been back to Senegal for twenty years. She had always found some reason or other not to go: work, money, her husband’s health, then his death, then other people’s children she looked after at school. The truth was she was afraid. Afraid of recognising nothing. Afraid that the city of her childhood no longer existed, and that nobody would remember her. Some fears, she said, you keep like family jewels.

Moussa was waiting for them at the airport, with a borrowed car and a huge smile. He had lived in Dakar for ten years; he was an engineer with a telecommunications company. He had organised everything, of course, in coordination with his sister, who had sent him a four-page spreadsheet. He had booked a small hotel near the corniche, overlooking the ocean, and had told each of his mother’s cousins, neighbours and old friends.

Getting off the plane, the heat hit them like a door opening onto an oven. It was thirty-two degrees, in the middle of December. Bertrand was wearing his grey suit. After ten minutes he was dripping with sweat. Amina looked at him, then declared that the honeymoon spreadsheet contained a serious error. The next morning, at the market, Moussa had him buy a light, embroidered midnight-blue boubou. Bertrand didn’t take it off all week.

Moussa lived with his wife, Aïssatou, and their three children in a white house in a quiet neighbourhood in the north of the city. Aïssatou was a doctor at the main hospital. The children, aged between six and twelve, had never seen their grandmother in person. They had only seen her on video, on Sundays. When Mariama walked into the house, they hid behind their mother. An hour later they were sitting on her knees, all three at once.

On the first evening, Mariama wanted to go straight to the port. She didn’t want to wait. Moussa tried to explain that the port had changed a lot, that there were fences now, guards, containers, that not just anyone could go in. Mariama replied that she wasn’t just anyone. She was the daughter of Ousmane Diallo, a docker on quay number four for thirty years. Moussa didn’t insist.

At the guard post, a man in uniform asked them what they wanted. Mariama spoke to him in Wolof for a long time, with a teacher’s authority no guard could ignore. The man listened, then phoned someone. Ten minutes later, an old man arrived, limping, leaning on a cane. He looked at Mariama. Then he said her name. He had worked with her father in 1978. He remembered the little girl with the mess tin.

His name was Ibrahima. He was eighty-two. He took them there himself, on foot, very slowly, to quay number four. The quay had changed, of course. There were huge cranes, containers of every colour, floodlights lighting up the night like day. But the sea was the same. And at the end of the quay there was still an old iron bollard, rusty, covered in flaking paint, on which Ibrahima placed his hand.

It was here, he said. It was exactly here that the French ship had moored in 1978. The sailor with the harmonica was sitting up there, on deck, at that height. And the little girl was here, next to the bollard, with her mess tin. Mariama went up to the bollard. She touched it. She closed her eyes. Nobody said anything. Then Bertrand opened his violin case, took Gérard Thiébaut’s bow, and played the first three notes of the waltz.

As they walked, Ibrahima told them what he remembered of that evening in 1978. The sailor with the harmonica spoke little. He was missing two fingers on his left hand, and Ibrahima had wondered how he could play. The other sailor, the young one, laughed all the time and threw cigarettes to the dockers from the deck. Ibrahima had caught one. He had never smoked it. He had kept it for years in a box, without knowing why, until it crumbled to dust.

The sound of the violin was lost in the noise of the port, among the cranes and engines. But Ibrahima recognised it. His eyes filled with tears. He said he had never forgotten that music either, and that for years, every time a French ship arrived, he had hoped to hear the harmonica again. He never had. Everyone keeps something, he added. He had kept that.

At the moment of silence, Bertrand stopped playing. Eight bars. Amina had brought her little silver triangle, the wedding one. She struck it once, in the middle of the silence. And Mariama, standing by the bollard, sang the next three notes in Wolof, as at the wedding party. Her voice carried far over the black water. On a neighbouring cargo ship, two Filipino sailors leaned over the rail to listen. They applauded.

The next day, Amina called Yves Le Goff in Brittany to tell him. She put him on speaker. Ibrahima, sitting beside her on a bench in the port, talked to the old Breton sailor. They had seen each other only once, fifty-six years earlier, one on a quay, the other on a deck. Yves remembered the cigarettes. He burst out laughing. Then he told Ibrahima he still owed him a cigarette, and that he would come and bring it to him himself, if he lived long enough.

That same evening, Ibrahima invited them to his home, a little house near the port, where he lived with his wife, his two sons and a dozen grandchildren. Ibrahima’s wife had made chicken yassa, with onions and lemon, so good that Bertrand had three helpings, despite Amina’s looks. After the meal, Ibrahima took an old tin box out of a drawer. It was empty. It was the box in which he had kept Yves’s cigarette.

In the following days, Mariama rediscovered her city. Not all of it: some neighbourhoods were unrecognisable, others had disappeared. But her childhood home, in the Medina, was still there, with its blue door and the little tree in the courtyard. A family she didn’t know lived there. They invited her in. The lady of the house offered her tea, three times, as tradition requires, and Mariama cried in front of each of the three glasses.

She also found her old school, where she had learnt to read and had dreamt of becoming a teacher. The school still existed. It had been enlarged. But there was still no music room, no instruments, no teacher. The head, an energetic young man, explained that they had no budget for it. Anyone who wanted to learn music had to pay for private lessons, which almost nobody could afford.

Amina listened to the head in silence. So did Bertrand. They looked at each other. They didn’t need to speak. That same evening, at the hotel, Amina opened a new spreadsheet. It was called “Dakar”. She sent it to Julien at midnight, with a single question: could the “Musique en partage” network, which had already given its method to Bucharest, give it to a school in the Medina too? Julien replied at six in the morning. A single word: “Of course.”

One morning, Moussa took them to the island of Gorée, opposite Dakar, from which slaves were once shipped to America. They visited the House of Slaves, with its little door open onto the ocean, the door of no return. Nobody spoke. In front of the door, Mariama asked everyone to be even quieter. Eight bars. Not for the waltz, this time. For those who had passed through there. Bertrand didn’t take out his violin. He just bowed his head.

Amina’s “Honeymoon” spreadsheet, which had planned visits, beaches and restaurants, had been abandoned by the third day. It had been replaced by the “Dakar” spreadsheet, which contained names of schools, musicians, instrument makers and suppliers. Bertrand had suggested one evening that they take at least one day of real holiday. Amina had agreed. They spent it visiting a kora workshop.

They spent the rest of the honeymoon preparing the project. It may not have been an ordinary honeymoon, but neither of them would have wanted any other. They met the head three times. They visited two other schools in the neighbourhood. They found a musician, a kora player of about forty named Lamine, who taught the children of his street for free, in the evenings, under a mango tree, and who agreed to lead the future orchestra.

Lamine came from a family of griots, the musicians and storytellers who for centuries have kept the memory of African families in their songs. His grandfather had taught him the kora at five. He said a griot was a living library, and that when a griot died, a library burnt down. He had started teaching the children in his street so that the library wouldn’t burn with him. For free. Under the mango tree.

One evening Lamine played the kora for them under his mango tree, surrounded by about twenty children sitting on the ground. The kora is a kind of large African harp, made of a calabash and twenty-one strings. The sound was so soft, so clear, that Bertrand forgot to breathe. Then Lamine asked them to play something too. Bertrand played Henri’s waltz. Lamine listened to it once. The second time, he was playing it with him on his kora.

At the moment of silence, Lamine stopped too, without being told. He had understood on his own. The twenty children fell silent. Eight bars. Under the mango tree, in the warm December night, only the crickets could be heard. Then, across the street, an old woman at her window whistled something. It wasn’t Henri’s three notes. It was another tune, a Senegalese one. But it came at exactly the right moment.

They spent Christmas at Mariama’s elder sister’s, in a big house full of cousins, aunts and children running everywhere. Great-aunt Fatou, who had flown back from Lyon with them, presided over the table from an armchair and told everyone about the Lyon wedding, adding a new detail each time. At the end of the meal, Bertrand played the waltz. Everyone fell silent at the right moment. Fatou had explained the rule to everyone before they even sat down.

Before they left, Lamine organised a first lesson, to see how it went. About twenty children came under the mango tree with makeshift instruments: jerrycans, tin cans, bottles filled with sand, an old plastic recorder. Bertrand taught them the first three notes of the waltz on the violin. Lamine repeated them on the kora. Then the children beat them out on their jerrycans. It sounded like nothing at all. Bertrand said it was exactly like the first day of the Thursday orchestra.

On the last day, before catching the plane, Mariama went back alone to quay number four, with Ibrahima. She stayed there an hour. Nobody knows what she did there. When she came back to the hotel, her eyes were red, but she was smiling. She told Amina she would come back in the spring to help launch the orchestra. Then she added that she had decided to retire. In Dakar. To teach music, this time.

Meanwhile, in Lyon, Julien had received an unexpected call. It was the chief curator of the Lyon Museum of Fine Arts, a woman of about fifty named Claudine Lacroix. Like everyone else, she had followed the story of the waltz: the video of the silence, the Corsican tree, the sailor from Dakar. She was proposing to organise an exhibition. Not about the network, she specified. About the waltz itself. About a tune that had travelled across half a century.

At the same time, the network’s board had examined the Dakar project. It would be the second school abroad, after Bucharest. The members had asked several questions: about the budget, the distance, the language. Amina had answered each one with a spreadsheet, from Dakar, by video, in a boubou. The project was adopted unanimously. One member asked whether the network would end up with schools all over the world. Amina replied: “Not everywhere. Only where someone is waiting for the rest.”

Julien refused at first. He said it was only a waltz, written by a sailor who couldn’t even read music, and that nobody would want to see an exhibition about a harmonica and a cassette. Mrs Lacroix smiled on the phone. She said museums were full of far more ordinary objects: spoons, combs, shoes. What mattered was never the object. It was what had been done with it. Julien promised to think about it.

He talked to Isabelle about it. Isabelle said yes at once. She had kept all the objects of the story in Odile’s flat without knowing what to do with them: Henri’s twenty-three logbooks, the 1962 lime flower, the score of the waltz written out by Odile, the blue shawl, the armchair. She had long thought these objects didn’t really belong to her. That they belonged to everyone who had ever whistled the three notes.

Isabelle spent several evenings sorting through her mother’s things. It was harder than she had expected. In every drawer there was something she had forgotten: a letter from Henri, concert tickets, a shopping list in Odile’s handwriting with a musical note drawn in pencil at the bottom. Isabelle often cried. Rose-Hélène would cross the landing, sit down beside her, and sort with her, without a word, putting each paper in a different box.

Rose-Hélène set just one condition. Henri’s harmonica could go to the museum, fine. But not forever. Only for the exhibition. And she wanted to be able to come and see it whenever she liked, free of charge, and even take it out to play the three notes, if anyone in the museum needed it. Mrs Lacroix, to whom Julien passed on the condition, replied that no museum in the world had ever accepted such a clause. Then she accepted it.

The preparation took two months. Mrs Lacroix came to rue d’Austerlitz twice a week, with a team of three, white gloves and special boxes. She examined every object as if it were a Renaissance work. She photographed every page of the logbooks. She measured the blue shawl. She asked Isabelle to tell her the story of each object, and wrote everything down in a little black notebook.

In Mrs Lacroix’s team there was a young paper restorer, Léa, twenty-six, who had spent three weeks on Henri’s logbooks. Some pages had got wet at sea in the seventies. Others were stuck together with salt. Léa separated them one by one, with a brush and infinite patience. One evening she called Isabelle. Between two stuck pages she had found a lock of hair tied with a red thread. With a date: 1974.

Isabelle understood at once. 1974 was the year she was born. That hair was hers, baby hair, which Henri had taken to sea in his logbook on his long voyages. He had never told her. Isabelle asked for the lock to stay in the logbook, in its place, for the exhibition. But she also asked that it not be mentioned on any label. She said some things had to stay between a father and his daughter.

Then she began to look elsewhere. She wrote to Yves Le Goff, who lent her the original Dakar cassette and Henri’s old copper lighter. She wrote to Gérard Thiébaut, who sent her Yanis’s little note, “He has a difficult character, but he sings well”. She wrote to Corsica, to Marie-Ange, who sent her a burnt branch of the lime tree that had fallen during the winter, and Rose-Hélène’s thirty drawings that had dried on the wash-house wall.

She wrote to Bucharest too. Viorica sent her, by post, her father’s letter found in the piano, with a condition similar to Rose-Hélène’s: that it be returned before the summer, so she could put it back in the piano once it was repaired. And Mariama, back from Dakar, entrusted the museum with the 1978 photo of the little girl with the mess tin, with the blurred silhouette of a sailor in the background. Mrs Lacroix said it was the centrepiece of the exhibition.

Viorica’s letter arrived from Bucharest in a large envelope, with her father’s letter and a short note for Mrs Lacroix written in violet ink. In it Viorica said she was entrusting the museum with the most precious thing she owned, and that she did so gladly, because she knew thousands of people would read it. She added that her father, who had taught all his life, would have been happy to have so many pupils at last.

That left choosing the title. Mrs Lacroix had suggested several titles, all very beautiful, all very learned: “The Sailor’s Waltz: Memory and Transmission”, “A Tune Across the Century”. Nobody was convinced. It was Rose-Hélène, once again, who found it. One evening at dinner she asked why they didn’t simply call it after the most important thing in the waltz. Julien asked what that was. She replied: “The silence.”

So the exhibition was called “Eight Bars”. It opened on Saturday 10 February 2035 at the Museum of Fine Arts, in a large first-floor room in the middle of which Odile’s armchair had been placed, covered with the blue shawl, under a single spotlight. Around the armchair, in display cases, the objects of the story. And at the back of the room, on a white wall, in large black letters, a single sentence, in French, Romanian, Corsican and Wolof.

It was Odile’s sentence, the one she had written in her letter to Julien: “If one day you hear whistling on the other side of the landing, don’t look for who it is. Answer.” Mrs Lacroix had hesitated to put it up. She thought a single sentence on a wall was not much for an exhibition. Isabelle had replied that it was exactly the opposite: that anyone who needed more than one sentence had understood nothing about the waltz.

On the eve of the opening, late in the evening, Julien called in at the museum. Mrs Lacroix was alone in the room, adjusting a last spotlight. Odile’s armchair was already in place, in the middle, with the blue shawl. Julien stopped at the entrance. He couldn’t move forward. Mrs Lacroix switched off all the lights except the one on the armchair. Then she went out without a word and left Julien alone with it for ten minutes.

On opening day there was a crowd. Everyone who had played a part in the story had come, or almost everyone. Yves Le Goff, ninety-one, in a wheelchair for the first time, pushed by Nathalie. Gérard Thiébaut, eighty-two, who had taken the train alone from Mirecourt. Mrs Roux, eighty-eight. Mariama and Amina. Bertrand with his violin. The Thursday ducks, every one of them. And about a hundred strangers who had come from anywhere and everywhere.

Elena and Dan had come from Iași for the occasion, with a recorded message from Grandma, who was eighty-nine and no longer travelled. Minister Desforges was there too, discreetly, at the back of the room, with his daughter Clémence, who had brought her violin. And Inès, seventeen now, had come with Sami and Yanis, her lifelong friends, who had grown up with the waltz the way others grow up with a family song.

Henri-Ion, who was four, wasn’t looking at any display case. He was running from one end of the room to the other, sliding on the polished parquet, under the worried eyes of the guards. Then, all of a sudden, he stopped in front of Odile’s armchair. He looked at it for a long time. And for the first time in his life he whistled the three notes, all three of them, in tune, without any air, perfectly. Rose-Hélène turned round, astonished. Her little brother had just done in a second what had taken her two years to learn.

Some visitors cried in front of the display cases. Others took photos. An old lady stood for twenty minutes in front of the 1962 lime flower, without moving, holding her husband’s hand. A teenager asked a guard whether he was allowed to whistle in the museum. The guard, who had been told, replied that in that room, yes, it was even recommended. The teenager whistled three notes. Someone on the other side of the room answered.

Mariama stopped for a long time in front of her own photo, the one of the little girl with the mess tin. She had never seen herself exhibited in a museum. A visitor beside her read the label aloud: “A little girl on quay number four, port of Dakar, 1978. In the background, on deck, Henri plays the waltz.” The visitor turned to Mariama and said the little girl seemed to be listening with her whole body. Mariama replied: “It’s true. I remember.”

The visitor didn’t understand at first. Then she looked at the photo, then at Mariama, then at the photo again. She put her hand to her mouth. She said she couldn’t believe it. Mariama smiled. She said nobody believed it, and that she herself had taken fifty-six years to remember. Then she whistled the first three notes, softly, in front of her own photo. And the visitor, a stranger, whistled the next three.

Yves Le Goff had himself wheeled to the display case where the Dakar cassette lay, next to the copper lighter. He stayed in front of it for a long time, in his wheelchair, without a word. Then he asked Nathalie to bring him closer to the glass. He pressed his forehead against it, like a child in front of a toy shop. He murmured something only Nathalie heard. She said later it was: “Henri, stop that thing of yours.”

At the entrance to the room there was a large visitors’ book, open on a stand. From the first day it filled with messages in every language. In French, Romanian, Wolof, Corsican, Arabic, English, Japanese. Some wrote long letters. Others only three musical notes drawn on the page. Someone had written, in a child’s clumsy letters: “I whistled too.” Amina made a spreadsheet of the languages. By the end of the exhibition there were forty-one.

Around three o’clock, Elena played Grandma’s message on a small speaker. It lasted a minute. Grandma spoke in Romanian, in a tired but clear voice. She said she was too old to travel, but that she was there all the same, in the room, like Odile, like Henri, like Antoine. Then she whistled the three notes. Off-key. The whole room answered. Grandma never knew, but that day two hundred people answered her.

At four o’clock, Mrs Lacroix asked for silence for a short speech. She thanked the lenders, the families, the city. Then she said something nobody expected from a museum curator. She said that for two months she had handled objects with white gloves, and had understood that these objects had no value. An old harmonica, a worn cassette, a dried flower. No antique dealer would give ten euros for them.

“And yet,” she went on, “I have never organised a more precious exhibition. Because what matters here isn’t the objects. It’s what lies between them. The eight-bar silence that each of you has filled one day. Corsicans, Romanians, Bretons, Senegalese, Lyonnais. All these people who didn’t know each other, and who answered one another.” She fell silent. Then she said: “I leave you the silence.”

And the whole room fell silent. Two hundred people, standing around Odile’s armchair, in a museum, on a Saturday afternoon. Nothing could be heard except the ventilation and, somewhere in the building, distant footsteps. Rose-Hélène walked up to the display case where Henri’s harmonica lay. A guard, who knew about the clause, opened it for her with a key. Rose-Hélène took the harmonica. She played the three notes in the silence of the museum.

Then she waited. And it wasn’t Julien, nor Isabelle, nor Mariama who answered. It was an old man at the back of the room whom nobody knew. He whistled the next three, off-key, trembling. Then someone else carried on. Then someone else again. Each one took up where the previous one had stopped, like a chain, and the waltz went round the room, from one stranger to another, up to the silence of the third verse.

There, everyone stopped. Nobody had asked. Nobody had given a signal. But everyone knew. Eight bars. And in the middle, on the fifth, a little silver sound: Amina had struck her triangle. Then Bertrand raised Gérard Thiébaut’s bow and played the end of the waltz. Alone. In the middle of two hundred people crying, laughing, holding hands without knowing each other, in a museum room.

Rose-Hélène put the harmonica back in the display case herself, very carefully. The guard locked it. Then she turned to Mrs Lacroix and asked whether, now that the harmonica was in the museum, it still belonged to anyone. Mrs Lacroix thought for a long time. She said that legally it still belonged to the family. But that really, after what she had just seen, she thought it belonged to anyone at all. To whoever knew how to answer.

On the evening of the opening, Julien received a message from Bucharest. It was Andrei. Mr Petrescu had finished Viorica’s piano earlier than planned. It would be ready in May. It would be put back in the house through the balcony window, the way it had come out. And Viorica had already chosen the first piece to be played on it. It wouldn’t be a Chopin waltz, like her father’s. It would be Henri’s waltz. Andrei asked whether someone from Lyon could come and play it.

The “Eight Bars” exhibition was supposed to last three months. It lasted eight. More than two hundred thousand people visited it. In the room, every day, at times nobody set, someone whistled three notes and someone else answered. The guards ended up counting the waltzes, the way Amina had counted the litres of water. By the end of the exhibition there had been four thousand six hundred and twelve. Not one had been played in tune. All of them were complete.

Reading: The text at the exhibition entrance

The panel at the entrance to the “Eight Bars” exhibition, written by Claudine Lacroix. Notice the indefinite pronouns and adjectives. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Huit mesures : une valse à travers le siècle
In 1978, in the port of Dakar, a Marseille sailor plays a waltz on an old harmonica. He cannot read music. No professional musician has ever heard him.
And yet, fifty years later, this waltz is played in several countries by thousands of people. Some play it on the violin, others on the kora, others simply whistle it.

Everyone knows its rule: at the third verse, everyone falls silent for eight bars. Then someone, anyone, takes up the melody again. Such is the tradition, born of an old lady who whistled on the other side of a landing.
Most of the objects gathered here have no market value. An ordinary harmonica, a worn cassette, a few notebooks, a dried flower. Each of them, however, tells part of the story.
Some were lent by the family, others by friends in Brittany, Corsica, Romania and Senegal. We thank all those who entrusted us with their memories.

In this room, every visitor is invited to do what no other museum allows: whistle. Whoever hears three notes may answer. For this waltz belongs to no one. Or rather, it belongs to each of us. — Claudine Lacroix, chief curator
(“pour la plupart” = for the most part)

Write (at least 220 words) in French the presentation text for an imaginary exhibition about your family, your town or a passion. Present the objects and the people who lent them. Use at least 8 different indefinites.
I used “certains… d’autres…” or “les uns… les autres…”.

She had several recipe notebooks. We are showing a few of them, open at the page she liked best.
Each of her grandchildren lent a memory. Such generosity touched us deeply.
Anyone who has known a grandmother like her will recognise here any object from their childhood.
